paragraphs: The paper studies how to represent and learn chord progressions, which help organize tonal music over time. Its starting point is that a useful model should account for how chords sound in relation to one another. The authors design a distributed representation in which ordinary geometric distances roughly track perceived differences between chords.

This representation gives graphical models a musically motivated space in which to describe chord dependencies. Model parameters are learned using expectation maximization together with the Junction Tree algorithm. The authors compare several model architectures using conditional likelihood on examples outside the training data, assessing how well the learned dependencies carry over to unseen examples.

Both the perceptual evidence and the statistical comparisons favor binary tree structures related to musical meter. These structures organize chord relationships hierarchically around the rhythmic organization of music. The finding supports meter as a useful guide for modeling chord dependencies, while the approximate correspondence between distance and perceived dissimilarity supplies a connection between the representation and musical listening.
icml-2005-a-graphical-model-for-chord-pr.tldr: A perceptually motivated chord representation and graphical-model comparisons support meter-related binary trees for capturing chord dependencies.

paragraphs: Text classifiers often learn from documents whose labels are incomplete or unreliable. BayesANIL addresses this by explicitly estimating uncertainty associated with labeling. Given a fully or partly labeled collection, it estimates the joint distribution of documents and class labels, allowing uncertainty in the training annotations to influence what the model learns.

The estimation procedure generalizes expectation maximization. Its iterations re-estimate the empirical distribution to strengthen feature values contributed by unlabeled documents and reduce the influence of noisily labeled examples. The resulting estimates can be used within standard classification models, making the approach a way to improve the information supplied to a classifier.

Experiments with two classification algorithms report considerable accuracy improvements on standard datasets. The evaluations include conditions with and without artificially added label noise, and with and without unlabeled documents. These results suggest that accounting for labeling uncertainty can help across several training conditions. They also motivate the possibility of reducing manual labeling effort, without establishing that careful annotation is unnecessary.
icml-2005-a-model-for-handling-approxima.tldr: BayesANIL models labeling uncertainty to improve text classification using noisy, incomplete, or fully labeled training data.

paragraphs: The paper asks which time points should be analyzed when an experiment aims to reconstruct signals that vary continuously over time. Analyzing every available observation can be expensive. The objective is to choose informative measurements so that the continuous curves can be estimated while reducing the cost of collecting the analyzed data.

The approach targets a particular experimental arrangement: each time point contains measurements of multiple signals, materials or observations are archived beforehand, and the expensive analysis happens later. An active learning algorithm repeatedly selects time points using uncertainty about the quality of the currently estimated curve as its objective. Thus, sampling decisions respond to the developing estimate.

Evaluations use both simulated signals and gene expression data. The reported results show that the algorithm performs well and can substantially lower experimental cost without losing information. This finding applies to the selective-analysis setting described by the authors, where archived material makes it possible to decide which time points to examine after initial collection.
icml-2005-active-learning-for-sampling-i.tldr: An active learning algorithm selects archived time points for costly analysis and can reduce experimental expense without losing information.

paragraphs: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction compresses data while trying to retain meaningful relationships between nearby points. The paper examines spectral methods such as locally linear embedding and Laplacian eigenmaps. Although these methods preserve certain proximity relationships on average, their objectives do not explicitly require local distances or angles to survive the compression.

The authors construct an embedding that maximally preserves angles among nearby data points. They begin with the bottom eigenvectors produced by either or both of the existing methods, then solve an additional semidefinite optimization problem. This extra problem is small, and its size does not depend on the number of data points.

The optimization also supplies an estimate of intrinsic dimensionality: the number of dimensions underlying the data's structure. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate the approach's merits. The contribution is therefore both geometric and methodological: it adds an explicit local-angle objective to spectral embeddings while extracting information about the dimensionality of the structure being represented.
icml-2005-analysis-and-extension-of-spec.tldr: A small semidefinite optimization extends spectral embeddings to preserve local angles and estimate intrinsic dimensionality.

paragraphs: Many methods that exploit unlabeled examples learn predictions only for the particular collection of points supplied during training. This transductive setting leaves a further problem: how should the learner classify an entirely new point? The paper addresses semi-supervised learning in which labeled and unlabeled examples must support predictions beyond the original collection.

The authors construct data-dependent norms for reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, the function spaces associated with kernels. These norms reshape the space to reflect the geometry of the available data. They also derive explicit formulas for the corresponding kernels, providing a concrete way to incorporate that geometry into a predictive model.

This construction turns transductive methods and standard supervised algorithms into semi-supervised learners. Unlabeled observations can therefore influence the structure of the learned function while that function remains applicable to previously unseen inputs. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across several classification tasks, supporting the usefulness of combining data geometry with kernel-based prediction beyond the training point cloud.
icml-2005-beyond-the-point-cloud-from-tr.tldr: Data-dependent kernel geometry lets labeled and unlabeled examples support predictions on points never encountered during training.

paragraphs: The paper studies how an agent can carry out several activities simultaneously within a Markov decision process. It assumes an action space with multiple degrees of freedom, giving the agent the capacity for concurrent behavior. New tasks are expressed as collections of subgoals with different priorities, so planning must account for their relative importance.

The central idea is to combine previously learned activities through coarticulation. Multiple degrees of freedom often allow several admissible, though suboptimal, policies for the same activity. This flexibility gives the agent alternative ways to pursue an activity while also committing to other subgoals. Concurrency can emerge by selecting compatible behavior from these alternatives.

The authors provide efficient approximate algorithms for computing such policies and assembling concurrent plans, and evaluate the approach in a simulated domain. The contribution shows how flexibility within learned activities can support their combination. Its scope depends on the stated action-space assumption and on the available policy alternatives, rather than implying that arbitrary activities can always run together.
icml-2005-coarticulation-an-approach-for.tldr: Coarticulation combines flexible policies for learned activities to pursue prioritized subgoals concurrently in suitable Markov decision processes.

paragraphs: A Bayesian network classifier requires both a network structure and numerical parameters. This paper investigates how classification changes when each is learned with a generative or discriminative objective. Separating these choices matters because a structure selected to describe the data need not be the structure that best supports accurate class prediction.

For parameters, the authors compare maximum likelihood with conditional maximum likelihood. For structure, they examine conditional mutual information, explaining away residual, and classification rate. Their experiments cover naive Bayes, tree-augmented naive Bayes, and Bayesian multinets across 25 datasets, allowing the study to compare the learning objectives across several network forms.

Structures selected discriminatively using classification rate produce the most accurate classifiers on almost half the datasets. However, this search is computationally expensive and feasible only for relatively small problems. Discriminative parameter learning also yields better classifiers on average than maximum-likelihood parameter learning. Together, these empirical results support classification-focused objectives while showing that the cost of structure search can constrain their use.
icml-2005-discriminative-versus-generati.tldr: Discriminative learning improves Bayesian network classification on average, but searching structures by classification rate is computationally expensive.

paragraphs: The paper develops an expectation-maximization-type algorithm for maximizing conditional likelihood. The relevant models contain hidden variables and use distributions from the exponential family. Conditional likelihood focuses estimation on the distribution of an outcome given the observed input, making the method relevant to discriminative training of models with unobserved internal structure.

The algorithm also has an interpretation as gradient ascent with automatically selected step sizes. Its design exposes a tradeoff between computation and guarantees that each update increases likelihood. This tradeoff makes the procedure more computationally feasible than an earlier conditional EM method, addressing the effort needed to obtain dependable optimization steps.

The work also provides a theoretical foundation for extended Baum–Welch algorithms used to train discriminative hidden Markov models in speech recognition. Experiments compare favorably with the method described as the current best alternative. The contribution combines a conditional-likelihood optimization procedure, an explanation of its relationship to gradient updates, and a theoretical account of an existing family of training algorithms.
icml-2005-expectation-maximization-algor.tldr: An EM-type method makes conditional-likelihood optimization more feasible by trading computation against guarantees of likelihood-increasing updates.

paragraphs: Hidden Markov models with fully connected transitions become expensive as the number of hidden states grows. Three central operations—computing an observation sequence's likelihood, finding its optimal state sequence, and learning model parameters—have quadratic time complexity in the state count. The paper targets this shared computational obstacle rather than just one inference operation.

The authors introduce Dense-Mostly-Constant transition matrices, a structured class of transition models that remains non-sparse. This structure enables algorithms for all three HMM problems whose dependence on the number of states is subquadratic. The approach therefore gains efficiency from the organization of transition values while retaining dense connectivity.

Experiments report dramatic speedups for likelihood evaluation, state-sequence estimation, and parameter learning. The DMC model also achieves strong accuracy and exceeds the tested baselines even in domains known to violate its assumption. Those findings show useful empirical tolerance of assumption mismatch in the evaluated settings, alongside the computational benefits obtained from explicitly adopting DMC transition structure.
icml-2005-fast-inference-and-learning-in.tldr: Dense-Mostly-Constant transitions enable faster HMM inference and learning, with strong accuracy and large speedups in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Maximum Margin Matrix Factorization offers a convex, infinite-dimensional approach to collaborative prediction. It provides an alternative to low-rank approximations and standard factor models, but its practical usefulness depends on how it is optimized. The paper addresses the computational barrier that arises when learning the model through a semidefinite programming formulation.

Standard semidefinite solvers available in the study could handle MMMF matrices with dimensions only up to a few hundred. The authors investigate a direct gradient-based optimization method and demonstrate it on large collaborative prediction problems. This changes the computational route used to fit MMMF, allowing the model to be examined beyond the sizes accessible to those solvers.

The evaluation compares MMMF with previously reported results for nine methods and finds that it substantially outperforms all nine. The stated finding concerns that comparison, while the broader methodological contribution is making a promising prediction model usable at larger scales. Efficient optimization is central here because it enables testing the model on problems that its standard formulation made difficult to handle.
icml-2005-fast-maximum-margin-matrix-fac.tldr: Direct gradient optimization scales maximum margin matrix factorization to large collaborative prediction problems and outperforms nine compared methods.

paragraphs: The paper extends skewing, an approach intended to help decision trees learn functions that are troublesome for conventional tree induction. Earlier versions applied only to binary variables. That restriction limited the kinds of input attributes the approach could directly use, even when a prediction problem otherwise called for a decision tree.

The new algorithm handles both continuous attributes, which take numerical values along a range, and nominal attributes, which represent categories. Its contribution is to broaden skewing's direct applicability beyond two-valued inputs. The authors evaluate the extension on randomly generated functions as well as real-world datasets, examining its classification accuracy across both kinds of evidence.

The reported results indicate that generalized skewing almost always outperforms a decision tree learner based on Information Gain in those evaluations. This supports the usefulness of extending the approach to richer attribute types. The claim remains an empirical comparison with that learner: the results show frequent gains across the tested problems without asserting that skewing improves every decision tree task.
icml-2005-generalized-skewing-for-functi.tldr: Generalized skewing handles continuous and categorical inputs and almost always beats an Information Gain tree learner in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: The Relevance Vector Machine is a sparse approximate Bayesian kernel method that produces predictive distributions, including uncertainty about its predictions. The paper investigates a counterintuitive behavior: its predictive uncertainty decreases as a test case moves farther from the training cases. The analysis therefore concerns the quality of uncertainty estimates, not merely the predicted values.

Inspired by a comparison with nondegenerate Gaussian processes, the authors propose augmenting the model to address this behavior. The resulting model, RVM*, primarily serves to support their theoretical and experimental analysis. It could be applied in practice, but the augmentation means it no longer retains the original model's true sparsity.

The experiments show a tradeoff in which sparsity comes with worse predictive distributions. This matters because a model's compactness and the reliability of its uncertainty estimates are distinct properties. RVM* helps expose that tension by changing the model in a way intended to repair its uncertainty behavior, while giving up the sparse representation that makes the original RVM attractive.
icml-2005-healing-the-relevance-vector-m.tldr: Augmenting the Relevance Vector Machine addresses its shrinking uncertainty away from training data but sacrifices true sparsity.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way for a reinforcement learning agent to create useful skills automatically by discovering subgoals. It seeks states that sit between two densely connected regions of the state space. Such states identify connections between regions and provide concrete intermediate destinations around which a skill can be organized.

To find these states, the method partitions state-transition graphs built from only the agent's most recent experiences. In these graphs, the relevant structure comes from transitions the agent has recently encountered. The discovery procedure therefore works with a local view of the state space instead of requiring a graph covering the entire environment.

The authors state that this local scope successfully identifies the desired kind of subgoal while keeping computational cost low. The contribution links the structure used to discover skills with the amount of experience processed during discovery. Its target is specifically states between densely connected regions, giving the method a clear structural definition of what makes a subgoal useful.
icml-2005-identifying-useful-subgoals-in.tldr: Partitioning graphs of recent transitions discovers subgoals between densely connected regions at low computational cost.

paragraphs: Independent Subspace Analysis seeks hidden groups of variables that are independent of one another, while allowing dependencies inside each group. It generalizes Independent Component Analysis by making an entire subspace the unit of independence. The paper introduces an algorithm for estimating these hidden subspaces from observed sample points.

The algorithm relies on estimating multidimensional differential entropy, a quantity describing uncertainty in a continuous multivariate distribution. It obtains this estimate using minimal geodesic spanning trees fitted to the samples. This gives the method a geometric way to assess multivariate uncertainty as part of identifying the independent subspaces.

Numerical studies include illustrative examples and an extension of the cocktail-party problem involving songs played by bands. Another example mixes independent subspaces whose internal sources are pairwise independent but still jointly dependent. That example highlights the distinction between independence of pairs and independence of a whole collection, which matters when identifying groups that may contain internal statistical relationships.
icml-2005-independent-subspace-analysis-.tldr: Geodesic spanning-tree entropy estimates support an algorithm for recovering independent subspaces that can contain internally dependent sources.

paragraphs: Sequence models often need to choose an output that satisfies relationships extending beyond neighboring positions. The paper explains that Viterbi inference, used for conditional random fields and hidden Markov models, does not naturally incorporate general nonlocal or nonsequential constraints. These requirements call for an inference procedure that can express broader output structure.

The authors formulate inference using integer linear programming and extend conditional random fields to support general constraints naturally and efficiently. This makes constraints part of the output-selection problem itself. When the constraints are sequential, the formulation simplifies to ordinary linear programming, showing that the optimization requirements depend on the structure of the constraints.

Experimental evidence comes from semantic role labeling, a natural-language processing task. The contribution is an inference framework for combining a model's predictions with constraints over the output sequence. The sequential special case also clarifies that introducing a general optimization formulation does not mean every supported problem requires integer optimization.
icml-2005-integer-linear-programming-inf.tldr: Integer linear programming enables CRF inference with general output constraints and simplifies to linear programming for sequential constraints.

paragraphs: The paper addresses text classification when categories form a hierarchy and a document may belong to several categories simultaneously. These two properties make the output more structured than a single class label. The proposed kernel-based model represents the hierarchy explicitly while allowing multiple category assignments for the same document.

The model adapts the Maximum Margin Markov Network framework. It expresses the classification hierarchy as a Markov tree with an exponential-family specification on its edges. To train it efficiently, the authors use incremental conditional gradient ascent in subspaces associated with individual examples and their marginal dual variables, organizing optimization around smaller updates.

Experiments show that training is feasible for datasets containing thousands of examples and hierarchies containing hundreds of nodes. Predictive accuracy is competitive with other recently introduced methods for hierarchical multi-category or multilabel classification. The result supports the practicality of combining a structured representation of category relationships with an optimization procedure that can handle the tested training and hierarchy sizes.
icml-2005-learning-hierarchical-multi-ca.tldr: A kernel-based structured classifier handles multiple labels in category hierarchies with feasible training and competitive predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model's structure becomes difficult when some variables are hidden. Relationships that involve those variables cannot be checked directly in the observed data. The paper focuses on identifying d-separations, the graphical relationships that encode conditional independence and help determine how a model's variables can be connected.

The authors introduce distribution-free techniques for identifying these relationships in continuous latent-variable models. Their setting allows nonlinear dependencies among the hidden variables. The contribution therefore addresses structural identification without restricting the hidden relationships to linear dependencies, while describing the techniques as independent of a prescribed distributional form.

The significance lies in finding an indirect route to structural information that direct conditional-independence checks involving hidden variables cannot supply. Identifying d-separations provides information about the graphical structure even when the relevant variables are unobserved. The stated result is a set of identification techniques for this setting, rather than a claim that every possible latent-variable graph can be completely recovered.
icml-2005-new-d-separation-identificatio.tldr: Distribution-free techniques identify d-separations in continuous latent-variable models that allow nonlinear dependencies among hidden variables.

paragraphs: The paper develops algorithms for nonnegative factorization of tensors, which extend matrices to arrays with more than two dimensions. Its formulation includes nonnegative matrix factorization as the two-dimensional case. This places matrix and higher-dimensional factorizations within a common framework while retaining the requirement that the factors contain no negative values.

The authors derive two optimization approaches. One is a direct gradient-descent method designed to preserve positivity during its updates. The other alternates through repeated problems involving multiple rank-one components. These provide two computational routes to the factorization, with the nonnegativity requirement built into how the factors are obtained.

The paper motivates the framework through connections to latent class models in statistics, sparse image coding in computer vision, and model selection. These connections explain why a generalization beyond matrices is useful across different data-analysis settings. The stated contribution consists of the factorization algorithms and their application motivations, establishing a shared computational framework rather than reporting a quantified performance advantage.
icml-2005-non-negative-tensor-factorizat.tldr: Two algorithms extend nonnegative matrix factorization to higher-dimensional tensors, motivated by statistical modeling, image coding, and model selection.

paragraphs: The paper treats object correspondence as a learning problem: given two objects, estimate how points on one should map to points on the other. It seeks a dense point-to-point correspondence through a deformation field, a description of how the object must change to align with its counterpart across its points.

The authors compute this field using a modified support vector machine. An added penalty encourages points to map to similar points on the other object, giving the learning procedure an explicit correspondence requirement. This puts the matching objective inside the model used to estimate the deformation, with little engineering or domain-specific knowledge in the overall system.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance and demonstrate applications that include nearly photorealistic morphs of three-dimensional head models. These examples show the estimated correspondences supporting visible transformations between objects. The contribution connects a learned deformation field to dense matching, with the similarity penalty supplying the central requirement that makes the transformation meaningful as a correspondence.
icml-2005-object-correspondence-as-a-mac.tldr: A modified support vector machine learns dense object correspondences through deformation fields, including nearly photorealistic 3D head morphs.

paragraphs: A classifier can sometimes reduce the cost of errors by declining to make a prediction. The practical question is how to set the parameters governing that choice. This paper addresses a specific type of binary classifier with an abstention option, replacing ad hoc parameter selection with an optimization method based on ROC analysis.

The method considers three formulations: cost-based, bounded-abstention, and bounded-improvement. These organize the choice around an explicit cost objective or bounds concerning abstention and improvement. Having different formulations matters because a classification system's requirements can concern both the expense of mistakes and how much freedom the classifier has to withhold decisions.

The authors demonstrate applications that effectively reduce misclassification cost and validate the method using a ROC-building algorithm and cross-validation on 15 datasets. The optimality claim is tied to the specified classifier type and optimization criteria. The work supplies a principled way to choose abstention behavior within those formulations, supported by evaluations on real classification data.
icml-2005-optimizing-abstaining-classifi.tldr: ROC analysis optimizes a specific class of abstaining binary classifiers under cost, abstention, or improvement criteria.

paragraphs: The paper learns how a visual recognition system should move its attention between informative image locations. Its architecture has three stages. First, an information-theoretic saliency measure removes irrelevant local descriptors and identifies candidate locations. Second, a codebook matcher examines those locations and produces weak hypotheses about which object is present.

The third stage combines local evidence through attention shifts, forming sequences of descriptor-action pairs. A Q-learning procedure explores these sequences and receives evaluative feedback from decreases in entropy, reflecting reduced uncertainty. It learns to favor attention shifts whose resulting scanpaths are especially useful for distinguishing objects, including the geometry of those paths.

Evaluations use indoor imagery from COIL-20 and outdoor imagery from TSG-20. The results show a significant contribution from learning and better recognition accuracy and processing time than the standard local-descriptor methods compared. The findings support learning the order and spatial pattern of evidence gathering as part of recognition, alongside selecting informative local image descriptions.
icml-2005-q-learning-of-sequential-atten.tldr: Q-learning trains visual attention sequences that improve object recognition accuracy and processing time in indoor and outdoor image evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper studies cooperation among learning agents that each own and store their own training examples. This differs from a multiclassifier arrangement in which every classifier has access to the same data. The question is how agents with separate collections can exchange useful examples and improve both their individual predictions and their performance as a committee.

Each agent can evaluate itself and identify training data it no longer needs. Through bargaining, that data can become available to another agent that may benefit from it. The central idea is that an example's usefulness depends on the learner receiving it: data that adds little for one agent can still improve another.

The experiments report improvements in both individual-agent and committee performance. The authors interpret these results in relation to the ensemble effect, where combining learners can produce stronger performance than relying on individuals. The contribution connects that collective benefit with selective exchanges of locally held examples, showing how apparently unnecessary data can retain value elsewhere in the group.
icml-2005-recycling-data-for-multi-agent.tldr: Agents improve individual and committee performance by bargaining over training examples that one agent no longer needs but another can use.

paragraphs: The paper seeks a low-dimensional linear representation of feature vectors that preserves information useful for predicting class labels. This makes classification relevance the guiding objective for compression. The method estimates mixture models by maximizing conditional likelihood, tying the chosen representation to how well it supports the relationship between inputs and labels.

Mixture models provide the flexibility to approximate distributions to any desired accuracy. The authors state that using conditional likelihood ensures that the selected subspace retains the maximum possible mutual information between features and labels. An EM-like estimation algorithm fits the model, combining distributional modeling with the search for an informative reduced space.

Classification experiments with Gaussian mixture components compare favorably with related dimensionality-reduction methods. The framework can also use other exponential-family distributions for data such as binary or integer-valued features. Visualization experiments use Gaussian and Bernoulli mixtures. Together, these results illustrate a supervised reduction approach whose distributional components can be adapted to the type of data being represented.
icml-2005-supervised-dimensionality-redu.tldr: Conditional-likelihood mixture modeling learns low-dimensional linear representations that preserve information for class prediction.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether specialized multiple-instance learning algorithms offer consistent advantages over supervised learners on multiple-instance data. The question is motivated partly by a theoretical connection: concepts learnable with one-sided noise under the PAC framework can also be learned from multiple-instance data. That connection makes supervised methods worth examining empirically in this setting.

The authors compare supervised and multiple-instance versions of Diverse Density, Logistic Regression, nonlinear Support Vector Machines, and FOIL across datasets from several domains. Comparing paired versions helps distinguish the value of adapting a learner to the multiple-instance representation from differences between the underlying learning algorithms themselves.

No multiple-instance algorithm wins across all tested domains, although some consistently outperform their supervised counterparts. Assigning high costs to false positives can improve supervised performance, and in several domains a supervised algorithm beats every tested multiple-instance method. These findings show that specialized adaptation can help, but its benefit depends on the learner and domain; supervised alternatives remain empirically competitive in some settings.
icml-2005-supervised-versus-multiple-ins.tldr: Multiple-instance specialization helps some learners, but supervised methods outperform all tested multiple-instance alternatives in several domains.

paragraphs: Greedy decision tree learners can struggle with Boolean functions such as parity, particularly when the inputs include irrelevant variables. Earlier empirical work found that skewing could help these learners succeed. This paper investigates why that happens, focusing on whether skewing can identify the variables that actually matter to the target function.

The main theoretical result states that, in an idealized setting, skewing finds relevant variables with probability one for any function and choice of skew parameters. The idealized setting is essential to the scope of that guarantee. The result supplies a theoretical explanation for relevant-variable discovery without asserting identical behavior in every practical learning situation.

The authors also run experiments examining how parameter choices affect empirical success and analyze a variant called Sequential Skewing. These parts connect the theoretical result to questions about how the method behaves when used in practice. The contribution combines an explanation of skewing's ability to expose relevant inputs with an empirical investigation of choices that influence its effectiveness.
icml-2005-why-skewing-works-learning-dif.tldr: Skewing is proved to find relevant Boolean variables with probability one in an idealized setting, alongside empirical analysis of parameter choices.
